items.text: At the base of the status hierarchy among performers are cover bands, which are often accorded little critical artistic weight. <break time="0.8s" /> Reliance on someone elses material concedes that you have nothing of your own to say. <break time="0.8s" /> However, playing covers fulfills aesthetic, educational and economic roles. <break time="0.8s" /> Some covers take the original recording as a starting point and modify or reinvent it creatively. <break time="0.8s" /> Bands starting out rely on cover versions for a large part of their repertoire out of necessity, mastering them as part of a learning process. <break time="0.8s" /> Even original performers will usually play a few covers. <break time="0.8s" /> The distinction between cover and original is important, since upward career mobility is directly tied to notions of originality. <break time="0.8s" /> Learning such songs is part of the apprenticeship process in acquiring musicianship through engaging with a musical tradition. <break time="0.8s" /> An example is the development of rock in England in the 1960s through local bands covering imported copies of American rhythm and blues hits. <break time="0.8s" /> Cover songs are literally music to the ears of the managers of pubs and the like, as they are tapping into a proven product that the audience can identify with. <break time="0.8s" /> For each new generation of listeners, a good song is a good song.
